Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Mr. Johnson is a 61-year-old married man who has been driving buses in his city for over three decades. His life took a drastic turn when he was subjected to torture several years ago during a business trip abroad. Since then, the trauma has deeply affected his daily functioning and sense of self. The night still brings an overwhelming sense of vulnerability for Mr. Johnson. He finds it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, always listening intently for any sounds that might indicate someone is entering his home. This vigilance stems from a pervasive fear that echoes the terror he experienced during the torture. The event was so traumatic that remembering even parts of it can trigger strong physical reactions and bring back the same intense feelings of terror. Mr. Johnson’s memories are fragmented; some moments are crystal clear, while others remain blank. He feels as though there is an incomplete picture of what transpired, which leaves him with a nagging sense that he might be missing crucial details from his experience. This uncertainty exacerbates his distress and contributes to the negative self-appraisals that plague him. He harbors deep feelings of guilt for not having done more during the event to prevent or stop the torture. Mr. Johnson is consumed by thoughts of his own weakness, believing he should have been able to protect others from harm but failed in doing so. These beliefs feed into his heightened sense of threat and make it difficult for him to feel safe, even in familiar surroundings. The cycle that has formed over time reveals how these elements reinforce one another. The intense memories often resurface during the night, triggering physical reactions and increasing his vigilance. His belief that he is weak and unable to protect himself or others leads to a heightened sense of threat, further fueling his intrusive thoughts about what could happen again. This vicious cycle has left him feeling constantly on edge and struggling with daily tasks. Mr. Johnson’s occupation as a bus driver provides a stark backdrop for his symptoms. The noise and unpredictability of the city during rush hour can sometimes trigger his physical reactions, making it difficult to focus on driving safely. His wife has noticed that he becomes more withdrawn and anxious, particularly at night when he is hyper-vigilant. The relentless nature of these symptoms finally prompted Mr. Johnson to seek help. He is most afraid that the memories will never leave him and that he will continue to struggle with feelings of guilt and weakness. At the same time, he hopes for a way to regain some sense of safety and peace in his daily life. His primary goal is to find a way to manage these symptoms so that they no longer control his existence.
